{{Short description|Extension of a formal language by the epsilon operator}}
In logic, [[David Hilbert|Hilbert]]'s '''epsilon calculus''' is an extension of a [[formal language]] by the epsilon operator, where the epsilon operator substitutes for [[Quantification (logic)|quantifiers]] in that language as a method leading to a [[consistency proof|proof of consistency]] for the extended formal language.  The ''epsilon operator'' and ''epsilon substitution method'' are typically applied to a [[first-order logic|first-order predicate calculus]], followed by a demonstration of consistency. The epsilon-extended calculus is further extended and generalized to cover those mathematical objects, classes, and categories for which there is a desire to show consistency, building on previously-shown consistency at earlier levels.<ref>Avigad and Zach (2013), [https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/epsilon-calculus/#Over "Overview"] </ref>

==Epsilon operator==

===Hilbert notation===
For any formal language <math>L</math>, extend <math>L</math> by adding the epsilon operator to redefine quantification:

*<math> (\exists x) A(x)\ \equiv \ A(\epsilon x\ A) </math>
*<math> (\forall x) A(x)\ \equiv \ \neg \exists x \neg A(x) \leftrightarrow \neg \bigl(\neg A(\epsilon x\ \neg A)\bigr) \leftrightarrow A\bigl(\epsilon x\ (\neg A)\bigr) </math>

The intended interpretation of <math>\epsilon x\ A</math> is ''some'' <math>x</math> that satisfies <math>A</math>, if it exists.  In other words, <math>\epsilon x\ A</math> returns some [[term (logic)|term]] <math>t</math> such that <math>A(t)</math> is true, otherwise it returns some default or arbitrary term.  If more than one term can satisfy <math>A</math>, then any one of these terms (which make <math>A</math> true) can be [[Axiom of Choice|chosen]], non-deterministically.  Equality is required to be defined under <math>L</math>, and the only rules required for <math>L</math> extended by the epsilon operator are [[modus ponens]] and the substitution of <math>A(t)</math> to replace <math>A(x)</math> for any term <math>t</math>.<ref>Avigad and Zach (2013), [https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/epsilon-calculus/#EpsiCalc "The Epsilon Calculus"]</ref>

===Bourbaki notation===
In tau-square notation from [[Nicolas Bourbaki|N. Bourbaki's]] ''Theory of Sets'', the quantifiers are defined as follows:

*<math> (\exists x) A(x)\ \equiv \ \bigl(\tau_x(A)|x\bigr)A </math>
*<math> (\forall x) A(x)\ \equiv \ \neg \bigl(\tau_x(\neg A)|x\bigr)\neg A\ \equiv \ \bigl(\tau_x(\neg A)|x\bigr)A</math>

where <math>A</math> is a relation in <math>L</math>, <math>x</math> is a variable, and <math>\tau_x(A)</math> juxtaposes a <math>\tau</math> at the front of <math>A</math>, replaces all instances of <math>x</math> with <math>\square</math>, and links them back to <math>\tau</math>.  Then let <math>Y</math> be an assembly, <math>(Y|x)A</math> denotes the replacement of all variables <math>x</math> in <math>A</math> with <math>Y</math>.

This notation is equivalent to the Hilbert notation and is read the same. It is used by Bourbaki to define [[cardinal assignment]] since they do not use the [[axiom of replacement]].

Defining quantifiers in this way leads to great inefficiencies. For instance, the expansion of Bourbaki's original definition of the number one, using this notation, has length approximately 4.5&nbsp;&times;&nbsp;10<sup>12</sup>, and for a later edition of Bourbaki that combined this notation with the [[Kazimierz Kuratowski|Kuratowski]] definition of [[ordered pair]]s, this number grows to approximately 2.4&nbsp;&times;&nbsp;10<sup>54</sup>.<ref>{{citation

==Modern approaches==

[[Hilbert's program]] for mathematics was to justify those [[formal system]]s as consistent in relation to constructive or semi-constructive systems. While [[Gödel's incompleteness theorems|Gödel's results on incompleteness]] mooted Hilbert's Program to a great extent, modern researchers find the epsilon calculus to provide alternatives for approaching proofs of systemic consistency as described in the epsilon substitution method.

===Epsilon substitution method===
A theory to be checked for consistency is first embedded in an appropriate epsilon calculus. Second, a process is developed for re-writing quantified theorems to be expressed in terms of epsilon operations via the epsilon substitution method. Finally, the process must be shown to normalize the re-writing process, so that the re-written theorems satisfy the axioms of the theory.<ref>Avigad and Zach (2013), [https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/epsilon-calculus/#ReceDeve "More recent developments"]</ref>
